content.everyday_use: Fuel of the Sun and stars; part of every water molecule
content.go_deeper: About three-quarters of the normal matter in the universe is hydrogen. Inside the Sun, hydrogen nuclei smash together and fuse into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.
content.try_it: Every glass of water (H₂O) holds two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom: roughly 10²⁵ hydrogen atoms in a single glass.

check_question.question: What does the Sun fuse hydrogen into?
check_question.explanation: Fusion joins hydrogen nuclei into helium, and a little mass becomes a lot of energy (E = mc²).

content.everyday_use: Party balloons and cooling the giant magnets in MRI scanners
content.go_deeper: Helium was first spotted in the Sun's light in 1868, before anyone found it on Earth. It's so light it can escape our atmosphere, so we get it from natural gas wells.
content.try_it: Compare a helium balloon and an air-filled one over two days. Tiny helium atoms leak through the rubber much faster.

check_question.question: Why does a helium balloon float?
check_question.correct: Helium is less dense than air
check_question.explanation: Less dense gas means the balloon weighs less than the air it pushes aside, so it rises.

content.everyday_use: Rechargeable batteries in phones, laptops and electric cars
content.go_deeper: The lightest metal; it's soft enough to cut with a knife. When your phone charges, lithium ions move into one electrode, and they flow back out to power the phone.
content.try_it: Check the label on a phone, laptop or vape battery: it will say 'Li-ion' or 'Li-po'.

check_question.question: In a lithium-ion battery, what moves back and forth between the electrodes?
check_question.explanation: Charged lithium atoms (ions) shuttle between electrodes as the battery charges and discharges.

content.everyday_use: Lightweight, stiff parts in satellites and space telescope mirrors
Heat-resistant glass cookware and the borax used to make slime
Every living thing, plus pencil graphite and diamonds
content.go_deeper: Carbon can bond to four other atoms at once and form long chains and rings, so it's the backbone of every living thing. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, just arranged differently.
content.try_it: Draw a line with a pencil. You're leaving behind layers of graphite, sheets of carbon atoms that slide off each other.

check_question.question: Diamond and pencil graphite are both made of...
check_question.explanation: Same element, different structure: diamond is a rigid 3D network, graphite is slippery stacked sheets.

content.everyday_use: 78% of the air you breathe; fertilizer; the gas that puffs up chip bags
content.go_deeper: Nitrogen is 78% of air, but N₂ is so stable that plants can't use it directly. Factories turn it into ammonia fertilizer, which helps grow food for about half the world's people.
content.try_it: Squeeze a bag of chips: the cushion inside is nitrogen. It keeps oxygen out so the chips don't go stale.

check_question.question: About what percent of air is nitrogen?
check_question.explanation: Nitrogen ~78%, oxygen ~21%, argon ~1%, plus a little carbon dioxide.

content.everyday_use: 21% of the air; you need it to release energy from food
content.go_deeper: Oxygen is 21% of air and about 65% of your body's mass, mostly in water. Fire needs it, and rust is iron slowly combining with it.
content.try_it: With an adult, cover a lit tea candle with a glass jar. The flame dies once it uses up the oxygen inside.

check_question.question: Which gas do your cells use to release energy from food?
check_question.explanation: Cellular respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose; you breathe out the carbon dioxide made.

content.everyday_use: Cavity-fighting toothpaste and nonstick frying pans
content.go_deeper: The most reactive element of all. Fluoride in toothpaste swaps into tooth enamel and makes it harder for acids to dissolve. In nonstick pans, fluorine wraps carbon chains so food can't grip.
content.try_it: Read a toothpaste tube: look for sodium fluoride or stannous fluoride in the active ingredients.

check_question.question: Why is fluoride added to toothpaste?
check_question.explanation: Fluoride forms a tougher mineral in enamel that bacterial acids struggle to dissolve.

content.everyday_use: Glowing red-orange signs
content.go_deeper: When electricity runs through neon, its electrons jump to higher energy levels, then fall back and give off red-orange light. Every element has its own light 'fingerprint'.
content.try_it: Many 'neon' signs in blue or green actually use other gases or coated tubes. True neon is always red-orange.

check_question.question: Why does neon glow inside a sign?
check_question.explanation: Electrons absorb energy, then release it as light of colors unique to that element.

content.everyday_use: Table salt and baking soda
content.go_deeper: Pure sodium is a soft metal that fizzes violently in water. Bond it to chlorine, a toxic gas, and you get harmless table salt. Chemistry can completely change properties.
content.try_it: Old orange streetlights got their color from glowing sodium vapor, the same yellow-orange you see when salty water boils over onto a gas flame.

check_question.question: Table salt is sodium combined with...
check_question.explanation: Na + Cl → NaCl: sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine, forming ions that stick together.

content.everyday_use: Bright white sparks in fireworks and light bike frames
content.go_deeper: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light, perfect for flares and fireworks. A magnesium atom also sits at the center of every chlorophyll molecule, which lets plants capture sunlight.
content.try_it: Look at a green leaf: each chlorophyll molecule inside has exactly one magnesium atom at its heart.

check_question.question: Which plant molecule has magnesium at its center?
check_question.explanation: Without magnesium, plants can't make chlorophyll; their leaves turn yellow.

content.everyday_use: Soda cans, foil and airplane bodies
content.go_deeper: Aluminum is the most common metal in Earth's crust, yet it was once pricier than gold because it was so hard to extract. Recycling a can uses about 95% less energy than making new metal.
content.try_it: Squeeze an empty can: it's light and bendy, and an invisible oxide layer stops it from rusting.

check_question.question: Recycling aluminum saves about how much energy compared with making it new?
check_question.explanation: Melting old cans takes far less energy than separating aluminum from its ore.

content.everyday_use: Computer chips, solar panels, sand and glass
content.go_deeper: Second most common element in Earth's crust after oxygen. Ultra-pure silicon is a semiconductor: billions of tiny silicon transistors in your phone switch on and off to run every app.
content.try_it: Grab a handful of sand: much of it is silicon dioxide, the same stuff window glass is made from.

check_question.question: Computer chips are mostly made from...
check_question.explanation: Silicon can be tuned to conduct or block electricity, the on/off behind every bit.

content.everyday_use: Match heads, fertilizer and the backbone of your DNA
The smell of rotten eggs and the hardening of rubber tires
Keeping swimming pools and tap water germ-free
content.go_deeper: Chlorine gas is toxic, yet tiny amounts dissolved in water kill germs in pools and drinking water. It's also half of table salt.
content.try_it: That 'pool smell' mostly comes from chloramines, made when chlorine reacts with sweat and urine.

check_question.question: Why is chlorine added to swimming pools?
check_question.explanation: Chlorine destroys bacteria and viruses, which is why it made tap water so much safer.

content.everyday_use: The gas inside old-style light bulbs and welding shields
Bananas, potatoes and every nerve signal in your body
content.go_deeper: Your nerves fire by moving potassium and sodium ions across cell membranes. Every heartbeat and every thought depends on it.
content.try_it: Check a sports-drink label: potassium is one of the 'electrolytes' it replaces when you sweat.

check_question.question: Which element do your nerve signals depend on?
check_question.explanation: Potassium ions flowing out of nerve cells help reset them after each signal.

content.everyday_use: Bones, teeth, milk, chalk and seashells
content.go_deeper: About 99% of the calcium in your body is in bones and teeth. Seashells, chalk, marble and limestone are all calcium carbonate.
content.try_it: Drop a piece of chalk into vinegar. The bubbles are carbon dioxide released as the acid breaks down calcium carbonate.

check_question.question: Seashells and chalk are mostly made of...
check_question.explanation: CaCO₃ + acid → carbon dioxide gas + water + a calcium salt.

content.everyday_use: Extra-strong aluminum alloys in baseball bats and bike frames
Hip and dental implants, aircraft, and the white in paint and sunscreen
content.go_deeper: As strong as many steels but about 45% lighter, and your body doesn't reject it, so it's ideal for hip and dental implants. Titanium dioxide is the bright white in paint, toothpaste and mineral sunscreen.
content.try_it: Check a mineral sunscreen: titanium dioxide or zinc oxide is listed as the active ingredient.

check_question.question: Why is titanium used for bone implants?
check_question.explanation: Titanium forms a stable oxide skin that bone can grow onto.

content.everyday_use: Tough chrome-vanadium steel in wrenches and tools
Shiny chrome trim and rust-proof stainless steel
Steel making and alkaline AA batteries
Steel buildings and the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood
content.go_deeper: Earth's core is mostly iron. In your blood, iron in hemoglobin grabs oxygen in your lungs and delivers it to every cell. Steel is iron with a little carbon.
content.try_it: Crush iron-fortified cereal in water inside a zip bag, then sweep a strong magnet along the bag. Tiny black iron specks gather under it.

check_question.question: What does iron do in your blood?
check_question.explanation: Each hemoglobin molecule has four iron atoms, each able to hold an oxygen molecule.

content.everyday_use: Deep blue glass and phone battery cathodes
US nickels, stainless steel and rechargeable batteries
Electrical wiring and the coating on pennies
content.go_deeper: Copper conducts electricity almost as well as silver but costs far less, so it wires homes and electronics. The Statue of Liberty is copper; her green color is a protective layer that formed over decades.
content.try_it: Soak a dull penny in vinegar with a pinch of salt for 5 minutes. The dark copper oxide dissolves and it shines again.

check_question.question: Why is the Statue of Liberty green?
check_question.correct: Copper reacted with air to form a patina
check_question.explanation: Copper slowly reacts with oxygen, CO₂ and water to form green copper carbonates.

content.everyday_use: Rust-proof coatings on fences and white mineral sunscreen
content.go_deeper: A coat of zinc protects steel from rust because zinc corrodes first, sacrificing itself. Zinc oxide sunscreen sits on your skin and blocks UV light.
content.try_it: Look for dull gray, crystal-patterned coatings on fences and lamp posts: that's galvanized (zinc-coated) steel.

check_question.question: How does a zinc coating protect steel?
check_question.correct: Zinc corrodes first instead of the steel
check_question.explanation: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron, so it rusts away first.

content.everyday_use: LEDs and compact fast phone chargers
content.go_deeper: Gallium melts at 29.8 °C, below body temperature, so a chunk melts in your palm. Gallium nitride makes blue LEDs and small, cool-running fast phone chargers.
content.try_it: Check a phone charger box for 'GaN': that means gallium nitride inside.

check_question.question: What makes gallium unusual?
check_question.explanation: Its melting point (29.8 °C) is lower than body temperature (37 °C).

content.everyday_use: Fiber-optic cables and infrared night-vision lenses
Infamous poison in history; high-speed chips today
Dandruff shampoo and a trace nutrient you need
Flame retardants and pool sanitizers
Some high-speed camera flashes and insulated windows
Ultra-precise atomic clocks
Brilliant red fireworks
Red phosphors in old TV screens and laser crystals
Sparkly cubic zirconia jewelry and nuclear fuel tubes
Superconducting magnets in MRI scanners
High-strength steel for tools and engines
Medical scans that show how organs are working
Hard-drive layers and tough electrical contacts
Catalytic converters that clean car exhaust
Catalytic converters and dental fillings
Jewelry, mirrors and germ-fighting wound dressings
content.go_deeper: Silver is the best electrical and thermal conductor of all elements. Silver ions kill bacteria, so it's used in wound dressings and odor-resistant sportswear.
content.try_it: Silver tarnishes black when it meets sulfur in air or eggs. Clean it with aluminum foil, baking soda and hot water (with an adult).

check_question.question: Which element is the best conductor of electricity?
check_question.explanation: Silver beats copper slightly, but copper is used for wires because it's much cheaper.

content.everyday_use: Older rechargeable batteries and bright yellow pigments (toxic)
The clear conductive layer in touchscreens
Solder in electronics and the coating on food cans
content.go_deeper: 'Tin cans' are steel with a thin tin coating. Tin mixed with copper makes bronze, the alloy that gave the Bronze Age its name.
content.try_it: Solder that joins parts on circuit boards is mostly tin. Look closely at a circuit board's shiny silver blobs.

check_question.question: Bronze is copper mixed with...
check_question.explanation: Copper + tin = bronze; copper + zinc = brass.

content.everyday_use: Flame retardants and car battery plates
Thin-film solar panels
Iodized salt and antiseptic for cuts
content.go_deeper: Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make hormones that control your metabolism. Iodized salt was introduced to prevent goiter, a swollen thyroid.
content.try_it: With an adult, put a drop of iodine antiseptic on a slice of potato: it turns blue-black wherever there's starch.

check_question.question: Which gland needs iodine to work?
check_question.explanation: Thyroid hormones contain iodine atoms; without enough, the gland swells.

content.everyday_use: Bright car headlights and spacecraft ion engines
Atomic clocks that define the second
Green fireworks and X-ray 'barium meals'
Camera lenses and hybrid car batteries
Lighter flints and glass polishing powder
Welders' goggles and strong magnets
Super-strong magnets in earbuds, speakers and electric motors
content.go_deeper: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are the strongest permanent magnets. Tiny ones make earbuds, phone vibration motors and electric car motors possible.
content.try_it: The magnets that hold some phone cases or laptop lids are likely neodymium. Keep them away from cards and pacemakers.

check_question.question: Neodymium is famous for making...
check_question.explanation: A neodymium magnet can lift over 1,000 times its own weight.

content.everyday_use: Tiny nuclear batteries; historically, glow-in-the-dark paint
Heat-tough magnets in guitar pickups and motors
Glowing anti-counterfeit marks on euro banknotes
MRI contrast dye that makes scans clearer
Green colors in screens and lamps
Magnets in electric car motors and wind turbines
Medical lasers and magnet pole pieces
Amplifying internet signals in fiber-optic cables
Portable X-ray machines
Lasers and next-generation atomic clocks
PET scanner detectors and targeted cancer treatment
Tiny transistors inside modern computer chips
Small capacitors in phones and game consoles
Classic light-bulb filaments and drill bits
content.go_deeper: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3,422 °C, so it was used for glowing light-bulb filaments. Its symbol W comes from its other name, wolfram.
content.try_it: Find an old clear incandescent bulb: the thin coil inside is tungsten.

check_question.question: Why is tungsten's symbol W?
check_question.explanation: Several elements' symbols come from older or Latin names.

content.everyday_use: Superalloys in jet engines
The densest element; fountain-pen nib tips
Long-life spark plugs; the layer that marks the dinosaur-ending asteroid
Catalytic converters and jewelry
Jewelry, medals and connectors in electronics
content.go_deeper: Gold barely reacts with anything, so it never rusts or tarnishes; that's why ancient gold artifacts still shine. Your phone has a little gold on its connectors for reliable contacts.
content.try_it: About 10,000 to 15,000 old phones together contain roughly a pound of gold. Recycling electronics recovers it.

check_question.question: Gold's symbol Au comes from the Latin word...
check_question.explanation: Aurum means 'shining dawn' in Latin.

content.everyday_use: Old thermometers and fluorescent lamps
content.go_deeper: Mercury is the only metal that's liquid at room temperature. It's toxic, so mercury thermometers have mostly been replaced by digital ones. Hg comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, 'water-silver'.
content.try_it: If a fluorescent bulb breaks, air out the room and let an adult clean it up carefully: those bulbs contain a little mercury.

check_question.question: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
check_question.explanation: Mercury melts at about −39 °C. Gallium only melts at 29.8 °C.

content.everyday_use: Medical heart scans; toxic in large amounts
Car batteries and X-ray shielding aprons
content.go_deeper: Lead is dense and soft and blocks X-rays, which is why the dentist drapes a heavy apron over you. It was removed from paint and gasoline because it harms the brain, especially in kids.
content.try_it: Here's a twist: pencil 'lead' has never contained lead. It's graphite, a form of carbon.

check_question.question: What's actually inside a 'lead' pencil?
check_question.explanation: People once thought graphite was a type of lead ore, and the name stuck.

content.everyday_use: Pink stomach-relief medicine and rainbow crystals
Antistatic brushes for cleaning camera lenses
Cancer-treatment research; the rarest natural element
A radioactive gas that can build up in basements
Lab research only; extremely rare
Historic glow-in-the-dark watch dials
Targeted cancer-therapy research
Old camping lantern mantles; possible future nuclear fuel
Lab research only
Fuel for nuclear power plants
content.go_deeper: Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus releases tens of millions of times more energy than burning one carbon atom. Nuclear plants use that heat to boil water and spin turbines, producing about a tenth of the world's electricity.
content.try_it: Uranium is mildly radioactive and common in rocks; granite countertops contain trace amounts.

check_question.question: In a nuclear power plant, energy comes from...
check_question.explanation: Fission splits a heavy nucleus; fusion (as in the Sun) joins light ones.

content.everyday_use: Neutron detectors and research
Power sources for Mars rovers and deep-space probes
Household smoke detectors
content.go_deeper: Most home smoke detectors hold a tiny amount of americium-241. Its radiation lets a small electric current flow through air; smoke disrupts the current and sets off the alarm.
content.try_it: Look at the back of a smoke alarm for 'Am-241' (don't open it). Test the alarm button monthly.

check_question.question: How does americium help a smoke detector work?
check_question.correct: Its radiation lets current flow until smoke blocks it
check_question.explanation: Ionization detectors sense the drop in current when smoke particles enter the chamber.
